title: Open fracture of the tibia (BOAST open fractures)

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care

related.why: Recognising and acting on a threatened limb

brief.setting: Emergency department of a major trauma centre with an orthoplastic service
brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the trauma team
brief.scenario: Mr Kieran Doyle, 29, came off his motorbike at about 50 mph an hour ago. The trauma team's primary survey found an isolated injury to his right leg. The mid-shin is deformed, with a 5 cm wound over the front of the tibia and bone visible in it.
brief.task: The examiner will ask about your assessment and management of his leg, giving findings as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Open fracture: antibiotics within the hour, protect the wound, splint, check the limb, and the right theatre at the right time.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Washing the wound out in ED, or calling a high-energy injury a '24-hour' debridement.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "He's had his primary survey. I'll check the leg's circulation and nerves, then give IV antibiotics now."

grid.label: Limb assessment
grid.fail: Looks only at the wound; doesn't document pulses or nerves.
grid.pass: Primary survey first; then documents pulses, capillary refill, sensation and movement below the injury.
grid.high: Repeats neurovascular checks after realignment and splinting; watches for compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and on passive stretch.

grid.label: Antibiotics (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Holds antibiotics until theatre or a wound swab.
grid.pass: IV prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury, from the network open-fracture guideline.
grid.high: Checks allergy, gives them immediately in ED if the ambulance crew didn't, and doesn't wait for imaging.

grid.label: Tetanus
grid.pass: Treats a compound fracture as tetanus-prone; checks his immunisation; reinforcing dose if last dose over 10 years ago.
grid.high: High risk (soil, devitalised tissue, surgery delayed over 6 hours): also consider intramuscular tetanus immunoglobulin if his last dose was over 10 years ago.

grid.label: Wound care before theatre
grid.fail: Irrigates the wound in ED and keeps lifting the dressing.
grid.pass: Removes only gross contamination and photographs it; saline-soaked gauze under an occlusive film; realigns and splints the leg.
grid.high: Explains why: photographs in the record spare repeated inspection, and 'mini-washouts' outside theatre are not indicated.

grid.label: Timing of debridement
grid.borderline: Quotes 24 hours for every open fracture, missing that a high-energy injury needs 12.
grid.pass: High-energy injury: debridement within 12 hours of injury; immediately if highly contaminated or the limb's circulation is compromised.
grid.high: Contrasts low-energy open fractures (within 24 hours); knows NICE links high energy to likely Gustilo IIIA or IIIB.

grid.label: Orthoplastic plan and definitive cover
grid.fail: Plans orthopaedic fixation alone, with plastics 'if needed later'.
grid.pass: Consultant orthopaedic and plastic surgeons plan debridement, fixation and cover together.
grid.high: Definitive cover within 72 hours if not done at debridement; internal fixation only when cover follows immediately.

grid.label: Gustilo-Anderson classification
grid.fail: Can't classify, or grades on wound length alone.
grid.pass: Type I wound under 1 cm, clean; II over 1 cm without extensive soft tissue damage; III extensive damage, segmental fracture or traumatic amputation.
grid.high: Subdivides III: IIIA adequate cover, or any high-energy injury; IIIB soft tissue loss with periosteal stripping and bone exposure; IIIC arterial injury needing repair.

grid.label: Threatened limb (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Leaves a pale, pulseless foot until the morning list.
grid.pass: Pulseless foot after splinting: senior and vascular teams now; immediate debridement and revascularisation.
grid.high: Knows limb salvage versus amputation is a multidisciplinary decision with him and his family; delayed primary amputation within 72 hours.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you assess his leg?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: His primary survey's done. I'll document pulses, capillary refill, sensation and movement now, and again after realignment and splinting. I'd watch for compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and on passive toe stretch.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: IV antibiotics immediately, ideally within an hour of injury, from the network guideline, after checking allergies. I won't wait for X-rays or theatre.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's tetanus-prone. Last dose over 10 years ago means a reinforcing dose. If it were high risk, such as soil or devitalised tissue or surgery delayed over 6 hours, I'd consider immunoglobulin too.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Only gross contamination off, then photographs for the record so nobody needs to lift the dressing again. Saline-soaked gauze, occlusive film, realign and splint. No washout in ED; that belongs in theatre.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: When should he go to theatre?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He's high-energy: debridement within 12 hours of injury. A low-energy open fracture would be within 24. Immediately if heavily contaminated, like farmyard soil, or if the foot's circulation fails. NICE says high energy is likely Gustilo IIIA or IIIB.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A joint plan by the orthopaedic and plastic consultants. If cover can't be done at debridement, it should be within 72 hours, and internal fixation only when cover follows immediately.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Gustilo-Anderson: I under 1 cm and clean, II over 1 cm without extensive damage, III extensive damage. IIIA still has adequate cover, IIIB has soft tissue loss with periosteal stripping and exposed bone, IIIC has an arterial injury needing repair. High-energy trauma counts as at least IIIA whatever the wound size, so his is a III despite the 5 cm wound.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: After splinting, his foot is pale and pulseless.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Threatened limb: vascular and orthoplastic consultants now, and he goes to theatre immediately for debridement and revascularisation. If salvage were in doubt, that's a multidisciplinary decision with him and his family.

failures.move: Waiting for theatre or a swab result before giving IV antibiotics.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: deep infection risk rises with delay; BOAST sets as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury.

failures.move: Irrigating the wound in ED and repeatedly lifting the dressing to show colleagues.
failures.consequence: Adds contamination; BOAST and NICE say no washout before formal debridement in theatre.

failures.move: Scheduling a high-energy open fracture for debridement within 24 hours.
failures.consequence: Misses the 12-hour standard for high-energy injuries.

failures.move: Observing a pale, pulseless foot after splinting.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: the ischaemic limb may be lost; it needs immediate vascular and orthoplastic surgery.

recovery.line: Before anything else: IV antibiotics now, from the network guideline, ideally within an hour of injury.

recovery.when: You can't remember the Gustilo grades
recovery.line: What matters now is energy and contamination: high energy means debridement within 12 hours.

knowledge.fact: Antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour. Debridement: immediately if highly contaminated or vascular compromise; 12 hours high-energy; 24 hours low-energy. Definitive cover within 72 hours.
No irrigation in ED before wound excision; saline-soaked dressing with an occlusive layer.
Regimen in the 2009 BOA/BAPRAS standards: co-amoxiclav 1.2 g or cefuroxime 1.5 g IV 8-hourly; clindamycin 600 mg for penicillin anaphylaxis. Follow your network guideline.
High-risk tetanus-prone: heavy soil contamination, surgery delayed over 6 hours, or extensive devitalised tissue.

recall.think: Deep infection, a threatened limb, and compartment syndrome.
recall.say: "Open tibial fracture, high energy: antibiotics now, orthoplastic debridement within 12 hours."
do: Photograph, saline gauze and occlusive film; splint
Neurovascular checks before and after splinting
recall.trap: A 5 cm wound doesn't make it low-energy.
recall.finish: Joint orthoplastic debridement, stabilisation and cover.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

sources.name: British Orthopaedic Association and BAPRAS: BOAST Open Fractures (audit standards for trauma)
sources.supports: Long-bone open fractures go directly to, or are transferred to, a centre providing orthoplastic care (1); IV prophylactic antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury (2); a published network antibiotic guideline (3); vascular and neurological status documented and repeated, especially after reduction or splinting; suspected compartment syndrome per BOAST (4); limb realigned and splinted (5); arterial injury per BOAST arterial injuries (6); before debridement the wound is handled only to remove gross contamination and allow photography, then saline-soaked gauze and an occlusive film; no 'mini-washouts' outside theatre (8); photographs when first exposed, before debridement and at key stages, kept in the record (10); management plan by consultant orthopaedic and plastic surgeons together (11); debridement immediately for highly contaminated wounds (agricultural, aquatic, sewage) or vascular compromise, within 12 hours of injury for other solitary high-energy open fractures, within 24 hours for other low-energy open fractures (12); definitive soft tissue closure or cover within 72 hours of injury if not done at debridement (14); definitive internal stabilisation only when immediately followed by definitive soft tissue cover (15); limb salvage vs delayed primary amputation by multidisciplinary assessment with the patient and family (16); delayed primary amputation within 72 hours (17)

sources.name: NICE NG37: Fractures (complex): assessment and management
sources.supports: Do not irrigate open fractures of the long bones, hindfoot or midfoot in the emergency department before wound excision (1.2.20); consider a saline-soaked dressing covered with an occlusive layer (1.2.21); administer prophylactic IV antibiotics immediately in the emergency department if not already given (1.2.22); combined orthoplastic approach (1.2.27); wound excision immediately for highly contaminated open fractures, within 12 hours for high-energy open fractures (likely Gustilo-Anderson IIIA or IIIB) that are not highly contaminated, within 24 hours for all others (1.2.28); fixation and definitive cover within 72 hours if cover is not done at wound excision (1.2.29); consider photographing wounds when first exposed and before wound excision (1.3.5)

sources.name: UK Health Security Agency: Guidance on the management of suspected tetanus cases and the assessment and management of tetanus-prone wounds
sources.supports: Compound fractures are tetanus-prone wounds; high-risk if heavily contaminated with material likely to contain tetanus spores (e.g. soil, manure), surgical intervention delayed for more than 6 hours, or extensive devitalised tissue (7.2); IM tetanus immunoglobulin should be considered for high-risk tetanus-prone wounds (7.3); Table 4: adequate priming with last dose within 10 years needs nothing; last dose more than 10 years ago: immediate reinforcing dose of vaccine for a tetanus-prone wound, plus one dose of intramuscular tetanus immunoglobulin (or intramuscular human normal immunoglobulin as the alternative product) for a high-risk tetanus-prone wound

sources.name: Gustilo RB, Anderson JT. Prevention of infection in the treatment of one thousand and twenty-five open fractures of long bones: retrospective and prospective analyses. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976;58(4):453-8 (PMID 773941); with Gustilo RB, Mendoza RM, Williams DN. Problems in the management of type III (severe) open fractures: a new classification of type III open fractures. J Trauma 1984;24(8):742-6 (PMID 6471139)
sources.supports: 1976: type I open fracture with a wound less than 1 cm long and clean; type II laceration more than 1 cm long without extensive soft tissue damage, flaps or avulsions; type III open segmental fracture, open fracture with extensive soft tissue damage, or traumatic amputation. 1984 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6471139/): IIIA adequate soft tissue coverage of the fractured bone despite extensive laceration or flaps, or high-energy trauma irrespective of the size of the wound; IIIB extensive soft tissue injury or loss with periosteal stripping and bone exposure, usually with massive contamination; IIIC open fracture with arterial injury requiring repair

sources.name: Griffin M, Malahias M, Khan W, Hindocha S. Update on the management of open lower limb fractures. Open Orthop J 2012;6:571-577
sources.supports: Table 2 reproduces the BOA/BAPRAS 2009 antibiotic regimen: until first debridement co-amoxiclav 1.2 g 8-hourly or a cephalosporin (such as cefuroxime) 1.5 g 8-hourly; anaphylaxis to penicillin: clindamycin 600 mg IV in place of co-amoxiclav or cephalosporin

partner.opening: Mr Doyle has had his primary survey; the only injury is his right leg. How would you assess and manage it?

reveals.trigger: At the start, or when asked for his observations
reveals.finding: Airway clear, RR 18, SpO2 98% on air, pulse 104, BP 132/78, GCS 15. Pain 8/10.
Foot warm and pink; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable; capillary refill 2 seconds; sensation and toe movement normal. Calf soft.
No known allergies. Last tetanus vaccine at school, aged 14. No antibiotics given by the ambulance crew.
5 cm anteromedial wound with the fracture end visible; road grit on the surface; no farmyard or water contamination.
Comminuted mid-shaft fracture of the right tibia and fibula.

push.question: What is the time target for his antibiotics?
push.expect: As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury, from the network guideline.

push.question: When should he be debrided, and why that time?
push.expect: Within 12 hours of injury because it is high-energy; immediately if highly contaminated or with vascular compromise.

push.question: When does he need soft tissue cover?
push.expect: At debridement if possible, otherwise within 72 hours; internal fixation only with immediate definitive cover.

curveballs.prompt: He says he is allergic to penicillin: he had a rash as a child.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Ask what the reaction was and document it; a childhood rash isn't anaphylaxis. Follow the network guideline without delay (the 2009 BOA/BAPRAS regimen kept clindamycin for anaphylaxis).

curveballs.prompt: He came off his bike into a field of manure.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Highly contaminated: debridement immediately, and a high-risk tetanus-prone wound, so consider tetanus immunoglobulin as well as a booster.

curveballs.prompt: A colleague wants to flush the wound in ED because it looks dirty.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: remove gross contamination only, photograph and dress it; irrigation belongs in theatre.
